**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 20, 2026
**RE:** Baimix Live Holdings, LLC: Review of the Tinev Acquisition Documents, Issues and Recommended Fixes

---

## I. Summary

Baimix Live Holdings, LLC ("Buyer") bought the regional concert promotion and festival business of Tinev Concerts & Festivals, Inc. ("Seller"). The deal was done under an Asset Purchase Agreement (the "APA") that signed and closed on **January 12, 2026** (APA §3.1).

The Purchase Price was $30,000,000 (APA §2.5), paid as follows:

- $21,000,000 in cash at closing;
- a $3,000,000 indemnity escrow held by Calderline Trust Company, N.A.; and
- a **$6,000,000 Seller Note** issued by Buyer to Seller (Seller Note §1.1).

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder: the APA, the LOI, the Escrow Agreement, the Key Employee Agreement, the Seller Note, the October 6, 2026 Letter Agreement, the Lumora stage lighting rental agreement and Seller's closing officer's certificate. I found five issues. Two are time-critical:

1. **Most urgent: Orrant sale.** The pending sale of Buyer to Orrant Media Partners, L.P. is expected to close in December 2026. It will be an Event of Default under the Seller Note unless Seller gives its prior written consent. The file contains no such consent. On default, Seller can accelerate the full $6,000,000 note.
2. **Escrow claim.** Buyer's $1,150,000 indemnity claim (the July 20, 2026 notice) missed the escrow Release Date. It was also never sent to the Escrow Agent. The claim is therefore not secured by the escrow.
3. **Uncapped assumed liabilities.** Under the APA, Buyer bears unlimited liability for Seller's *pre-closing* breaches of the assigned artist, venue and sponsorship contracts. This is contrary to the LOI.
4. **Title claims now capped.** The October 6, 2026 Letter Agreement quietly removed title to the Purchased Assets from the "Fundamental Representations." Title and IP claims are now capped at $3,600,000 and expire after 18 months.
5. **Split forums.** The Seller Note's California law and Los Angeles forum conflict with the APA's New York law and New York forum. Note and setoff disputes would be split from indemnity disputes.

Two of these issues bear on the July claim and should be handled together:

- **Issues 2 and 3 overlap.** The sponsor make-good demands behind the July claim concern pre-closing activation failures. As drafted, APA §2.3(a) arguably makes those an Assumed Liability. That gives Seller a defense to the claim, and possibly a counter-indemnity claim against Buyer.
- **Issues 1 and 5 overlap.** Any setoff or withholding against the Seller Note will run into both the change-of-control default and the forum conflict.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Change of control under the Seller Note (pending Orrant sale)

**Where:**
- Seller Note §6.1(g) (Event of Default) and §2.1 (definition of "Change of Control," clause (a));
- Seller Note §6.2 (Acceleration);
- Letter Agreement Recital D.

**What the documents say:**
- **Default trigger.** Under Seller Note §6.1(g), it is an Event of Default if "Maker undergoes a Change of Control without the prior written consent of Holder."
- **Definition.** "Change of Control" includes any Person other than Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. acquiring, directly or indirectly, more than 50% of Maker's equity.
- **The sale.** Letter Agreement Recital D records two facts:
  - Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. signed a Membership Interest Purchase Agreement dated **September 22, 2026**;
  - under it, Baimix Group Holdings will sell **all** of Buyer's membership interests to Orrant Media Partners, L.P., with closing expected in December 2026.
- **No consent.** The Letter Agreement gives Seller's cooperation on Orrant's diligence only (§5). Neither it nor any other document in the folder contains Seller's consent to the change of control.

**Why it matters for Baimix:**
- **Default and acceleration.** Closing the Orrant sale without written consent will be an Event of Default. Under §6.2, Seller can then declare the entire unpaid principal of the **$6,000,000** note, plus accrued interest, immediately due.
- **Added costs.** Default interest at 8% (§3.2) and Seller's collection costs (§11.3) would also follow.
- **Knock-on effects.** An accelerated note could disrupt the Orrant closing itself and Buyer's senior financing. It would also give Seller leverage in the pending July claim dispute.
- **Subordination is limited protection.** Section 7 may delay payment while Senior Debt is outstanding, but §7.5 preserves Seller's remedies as between Maker and Holder.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Before the Orrant closing,** obtain Seller's prior written consent to the Orrant Transaction. Use a signed consent or a short amendment under Seller Note §9.3 that expressly waives §6.1(g) for this transaction.
- **If Seller will not consent on acceptable terms,** arrange for the note to be prepaid at the Orrant closing. Prepayment is permitted without premium under §4.5. The parties would need to decide how that interacts with any withholding for the July claim.
- **Coordinate with Orrant's counsel.** Make Seller's consent (or note payoff) a closing condition or deliverable under the MIPA.
- **Consider timing for leverage.** Pair the consent request with the other amendments proposed in this memo (Issues 3, 4 and 5).

---

### Issue 2: July 20, 2026 claim notice missed the escrow Release Date and never reached the Escrow Agent

**Where:**
- Escrow Agreement §4.1 (Claim Notices) and §4.2 (Release Date);
- Escrow Agreement §9.1 (notices to Escrow Agent effective only on actual receipt);
- Letter Agreement Recital B.

**What the documents say:**
- **Release Date.** Escrow Agreement §4.2 sets the Release Date at "six (6) months following the Closing Date." That is **July 12, 2026**. On that date the Escrow Agent releases the full Escrow Fund to Seller.
- **Retention rule.** The only amounts retained are the Claimed Amounts of Claim Notices "delivered to Escrow Agent prior to the Release Date."
- **Buyer's notice.** Letter Agreement Recital B records that Buyer's notice was:
  - **dated July 20, 2026**;
  - delivered only to Seller, at Seller's APA §11.2 address;
  - for **$1,150,000** of Losses for breach of APA §4.11 (Sponsorship Contracts).
- **Status of the claim.** Seller disputed the claim in full on August 14, 2026. Both parties reserved all rights.

**Why it matters for Baimix:**
- **The notice failed under the Escrow Agreement in two ways:**
  - it came eight days after the Release Date; and
  - it was never delivered to the Escrow Agent.
- **No escrow security.** The Escrow Agent was required to release the escrow to Seller on July 12, 2026, and nothing was held back for this claim. The $1,150,000 claim is therefore **not secured by the escrow**.
- **Escrow terms control.** Under APA §11.11, the Escrow Agreement controls as to its own subject matter. The APA's 18-month survival period (APA §9.1) does not extend the escrow.
- **What remains.** The claim itself is still timely against Seller under APA §9.1, and the reservation of rights in Recital B keeps it alive. It is now an unsecured claim against Seller, and Seller may hold few assets after the sale.
- **Effect on the Cap.** The claim is under §9.2(a), so it is subject to the $300,000 Deductible and the $3,600,000 Cap.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Confirm the escrow position.** Ask Calderline whether, and when, it released the Escrow Fund. The fees schedule suggests some balance-related activity may remain, so check this rather than assume.
- **Pursue Seller directly** under APA Article IX. Use the information exchange and meeting in Letter Agreement §6.
- **Use the Seller Note as security:**
  - Under Seller Note §5.2, Buyer may withhold the amount claimed from payments when due. Written notice to Holder has already been given.
  - The first principal installment of $1,500,000 falls due on **January 12, 2027**, so Buyer can withhold up to $1,150,000 from it.
  - This approach depends on resolving Issue 1 (no acceleration) and is affected by Issue 5 (forum).
- **Seek re-escrow.** Ask Seller to re-deposit the disputed amount under Joint Written Instructions, or to agree to a holdback. Add this to the change-of-control consent negotiation.
- **Going forward,** deliver every claim notice to the Escrow Agent, with a copy to Seller, before any escrow deadline. Calendar all release dates.

---

### Issue 3: Uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller's pre-closing contract liabilities

**Where:**
- APA §2.3(a) (Assumed Liabilities);
- APA §9.3(b) (Buyer indemnity for Assumed Liabilities);
- APA §9.5(c) (no Cap or Deductible on §9.3(b) claims);
- compare LOI §3(a).

**What the documents say:**
- **Assumed Liabilities.** APA §2.3(a) has Buyer assume "all Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts, *whether arising prior to, on or after the Closing Date*." The Assigned Contracts are the artist engagement, venue booking and license, and sponsorship contracts.
- **Buyer's indemnity.** Section 9.3(b) requires Buyer to indemnify Seller for all Losses from any Assumed Liability.
- **No limit.** Section 9.5(c) provides that §9.3(b) claims "shall not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible."
- **The agreed deal.** By contrast, LOI §3(a) says Buyer would assume "only liabilities under assigned contracts arising after Closing," and "not any liability arising from any breach, default, act or omission of Seller occurring at or before the Closing."

**Why it matters for Baimix:**
- **Unlimited exposure.** Read together, these clauses make Buyer liable, without any limit, for Seller's own pre-closing breaches of the assigned contracts. Examples include unpaid artist guarantees, pre-closing venue damage claims and sponsor make-goods. Buyer must also indemnify Seller if third parties pursue Seller for them.
- **No Seller backstop.** These liabilities are Assumed Liabilities, so they are not Excluded Liabilities. Seller's indemnity under §9.2(c) does not cover them.
- **Direct effect on the July claim.** The $1,150,000 sponsor demands relate to activation deliverables allegedly not performed *before* closing. Seller can argue that:
  - these are Assumed Liabilities that Buyer must bear; and
  - its exposure is limited to the §4.11 representation claim, which is subject to the Deductible and Cap.

  Seller could even assert a §9.3(b) counterclaim.
- **The LOI does not cure this:**
  - The LOI is expressly non-binding on this point (LOI §11).
  - It was overtaken by the signed APA.

  It is useful only as evidence of the agreed deal in negotiation, and possibly in support of a reformation or mutual-mistake argument, which would be uncertain.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Amend APA §2.3(a)** by written amendment signed by both parties under §11.6. The amended clause should cover only "Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts to the extent required to be performed after the Closing Date, excluding any Liability arising from any breach, default, act or omission of Seller at or before the Closing."
- **Add to APA §2.4** an express Excluded Liability for pre-closing contract breaches. That brings them within Seller's §9.2(c) indemnity.
- **Consider capping Buyer's §9.3(b) indemnity,** or at least excluding from it any Losses that are also a Seller representation breach.
- **Use the LOI as leverage.** Rely on LOI §3 as the record of the agreed deal, and bundle this amendment with the change-of-control consent.

---

### Issue 4: Letter Agreement removes title (§4.7) from the Fundamental Representations

**Where:**
- APA §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representations");
- APA §9.1 (Survival), §9.5(a) (Cap) and §9.5(b) (Deductible);
- APA §11.11 (Order of Precedence);
- Letter Agreement §3.

**What the documents say:**
- **Original definition.** The APA defines Fundamental Representations as §§4.1, 4.2, **4.7 (Title to Purchased Assets)** and 4.19.
- **Why the definition matters.** Fundamental Representations are carved out of:
  - the $3,600,000 Cap (§9.5(a));
  - the $300,000 Deductible (§9.5(b));

  and they survive six years (§9.1).
- **The amendment.** Letter Agreement §3 "amend[s] and restate[s] in its entirety" the definition to read "Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.19," which drops §4.7.
- **Precedence.** Under APA §11.11, signed letter agreements referencing the APA control first. Letter Agreement §7.2 also makes it a §11.6 written amendment, so the narrower definition governs.

**Why it matters for Baimix:**
- **Title is now a general representation.** Section 4.7 covers Seller's title to all Purchased Assets and its sole ownership of the festival brands, trademarks, domain names and ticketing/fan database. That is the core value in an asset deal.
- **Title and IP claims are now:**
  - limited to the **$3,600,000 Cap**;
  - subject to the $300,000 Deductible; and
  - barred unless asserted within 18 months of closing, that is, by **July 12, 2027**, rather than six years.
- **Undisclosed change.** This was not a negotiated business point. It sits in a document otherwise about supplemental domain names and post-closing consents. It is especially troubling because that same Letter Agreement transferred title-sensitive digital assets (Annex A) that Seller had failed to deliver at closing.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Reinstate §4.7** by a further written amendment signed by both parties. Restore "Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.7 and 4.19" with effect from the date of the Letter Agreement, so that no gap period exists.
- **Find out how the change happened.** Ask the client who negotiated Letter Agreement §3, and whether Seller's draft described it as a "conforming" change.
- **Interim protection.** Until the amendment is signed, have the client diligence any title or IP concerns now. Any §4.7 claim should be noticed well before July 12, 2027.

---

### Issue 5: Seller Note's California law and Los Angeles forum conflict with the APA

**Where:**
- Seller Note §10.1 (Governing Law) and §10.2 (Jurisdiction);
- APA §11.8 (Governing Law; Submission to Jurisdiction);
- APA §11.11 (Order of Precedence);
- Seller Note §5 (Setoff).

**What the documents say:**
- **The Seller Note** is governed by "the laws of the State of California." Note disputes must be brought exclusively in courts in the "County of Los Angeles, California."
- **The APA** chooses New York law. It requires any Action relating to the APA "or any Ancillary Agreement" to be brought exclusively in the County of New York. The Seller Note is a defined Ancillary Agreement.
- **Precedence.** APA §11.11 lets each Ancillary Agreement control as to its own subject matter. On that basis, the Note's California clause likely governs note disputes.

**Why it matters for Baimix:**
- **Two forums.** Seller can sue for note payments, or on acceleration (see Issue 1), in Los Angeles under California law. Buyer's indemnity claims, including the $1,150,000 July claim, must be litigated in New York under New York law.
- **Setoff depends on the other forum.** Buyer's setoff under Note §5.1 requires either Seller's written agreement or a final judgment, which would come from New York. Its withholding right under §5.2 would be tested in California.
- **Consequences.** The result is duplicative proceedings, higher cost, and a risk of inconsistent rulings on whether withholding was proper.
- **Default risk.** A California court could treat Buyer's withholding as a payment default. That would trigger default interest and acceleration.
- **No local connection.** Neither party has a California connection. Both are based in New York.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Amend Seller Note §10** under §9.3 to adopt New York law and the exclusive state or federal courts in the County of New York, consistent with APA §11.8 and the Escrow Agreement.
- **Add a provision** that note and setoff disputes may be joined with related Article IX indemnity proceedings.
- **Bundle this amendment** with the change-of-control consent (Issue 1).

---

## III. Documents with no issues noted

- **Key Employee Agreement (Okafor-Ruiz):** Customary terms, with New York law and forum. One point to flag for the Orrant transaction: §10.2 permits assignment to a successor. An equity sale of Buyer should not affect the agreement. Orrant may still ask about retention economics.
- **Lumora stage lighting rental agreement:** Unrelated vendor contract. Section 13.3 permits assignment without consent to a successor by sale of equity, so the Orrant sale raises no consent issue.
- **Seller closing officer's certificate:** It covers only APA §§4.1 and 4.2, consistent with APA §3.2(g). No issues noted.
- **LOI:** Non-binding and superseded, but relevant as evidence of the agreed scope of assumed liabilities (Issue 3).

---

## IV. Recommended next steps (in priority order)

1. **Immediately:** Approach Seller for written consent to the Orrant Transaction under Seller Note §6.1(g). Coordinate the timing with Orrant's counsel.
2. **In the same package:** Propose amendments to:
   - narrow APA §2.3(a) to post-closing obligations;
   - restore §4.7 to the Fundamental Representations;
   - conform Seller Note §10 to New York law and forum; and
   - re-escrow or hold back the disputed $1,150,000.
3. **Confirm the escrow position** with Calderline.
4. **Prepare to withhold** under Seller Note §5.2 from the January 12, 2027 installment, provided Issue 1 has been resolved.
5. **Calendar the deadlines:**
   - Orrant closing (December 2026);
   - first principal installment (January 12, 2027);
   - general representation survival expiry (July 12, 2027).

Please let me know if you would like me to draft the consent and omnibus amendment.

**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 20, 2026
**RE:** Baimix Live Holdings, LLC: Review of Tinev Asset Purchase Documents and Post-Closing Issues

---

## I. Summary

Baimix Live Holdings, LLC ("Baimix" or "Buyer") bought the concert promotion and festival business of Tinev Concerts & Festivals, Inc. ("Seller") under an Asset Purchase Agreement (the "APA"). The APA was signed and closed on **January 12, 2026** (APA §3.1). The $30,000,000 Purchase Price (APA §2.5) was paid as follows:

- $21,000,000 in cash at Closing.
- A $3,000,000 Indemnity Escrow held by Calderline Trust Company, N.A. (APA §2.6).
- A **$6,000,000** subordinated Seller Note issued by Baimix to Seller (Seller Note §1.1).

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder. I found four issues that need attention before the client takes its next steps. Two are time-sensitive because the sale of Baimix to Orrant Media Partners, L.P. is expected to close in December 2026.

| # | Issue | Location | Urgency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pending Orrant sale will trigger a Change of Control default and acceleration of the $6,000,000 Seller Note | Seller Note §2.1, §6.1(g), §6.2; Letter Agreement Recital D | **Immediate.** Must be resolved before the Orrant closing |
| 2 | July 20, 2026 claim notice missed the escrow Release Date and was not sent to the Escrow Agent, so the $1,150,000 claim is unsecured | Escrow Agreement §4.1, §4.2, §9.1; Letter Agreement Recital B | High |
| 3 | Letter Agreement drops Section 4.7 (Title) from "Fundamental Representations," so title and IP claims fall under the $3,600,000 Cap and the 18-month survival period | APA §1.1, §9.1, §9.5(a)–(b); Letter Agreement §3 | High |
| 4 | Assumed Liabilities include Seller's pre-closing contract liabilities, and Buyer's indemnity for them is uncapped, contrary to the LOI | APA §2.3(a), §9.3(b), §9.5(c); LOI §3 | High |

The stage lighting rental agreement with Lumora Stage Systems LLC and Seller's closing officer's certificate raise no issues relevant to these matters (see Part III).

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Orrant sale will trigger a Change of Control Event of Default under the Seller Note

**Where it appears**
- Seller Note §2.1 (definition of "Change of Control"), §6.1(g) and §6.2.
- Post-Closing Letter Agreement dated October 6, 2026, Recital D.

**What the documents say**
- **Change of Control.** Under clause (a) of the definition, a Change of Control includes any Person other than Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. acquiring, directly or indirectly, more than 50% of Maker's equity interests or voting power.
- **Event of Default.** Section 6.1(g) makes it an Event of Default if "Maker undergoes a Change of Control without the prior written consent of Holder."
- **Acceleration.** Section 6.2 lets Holder, by written notice, declare the unpaid principal and all accrued interest immediately due and payable.
- **The Orrant sale.** Recital D of the Letter Agreement records that Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. signed a Membership Interest Purchase Agreement dated September 22, 2026 to sell **all** membership interests of Baimix to Orrant Media Partners, L.P. Closing is expected in December 2026.

**Why it matters for Baimix**
- The Orrant Transaction falls squarely within clause (a) of the Change of Control definition.
- **Seller has not given its prior written consent.** No document in the folder contains it.
  - The Letter Agreement mentions the Orrant Transaction only in Recital D and in Section 5, which covers Seller's cooperation with Orrant's diligence.
  - Cooperating with diligence is not consent to the Change of Control, and nothing in the Letter Agreement waives §6.1(g).
- When the Orrant sale closes, Seller can accelerate the full unpaid principal (all $6,000,000 under the current schedule), plus accrued interest.
- Other consequences of the default:
  - Default interest at 8% (6% plus 2%) under §3.2.
  - Costs of collection, including attorneys' fees, under §11.3.
  - Baimix must give Seller notice of the Event of Default within five Business Days under §8.1.
- **Effect on setoff.** Acceleration would undercut Baimix's ability to manage the note payment schedule. In particular, it would complicate the use of §5.2 withholding to secure the July claim (see Issue 2).
- **Senior Debt.** If Baimix has Senior Debt, the default may also have consequences under those facilities. Those facilities should be checked.
- **Effect on the Orrant deal.** Orrant will very likely treat an unwaived acceleration right as a closing issue or a purchase price adjustment.

**Recommended fix**
1. **Obtain Seller's prior written consent** to the Orrant Transaction before it closes.
   - The consent should be a signed instrument that expressly references Seller Note §6.1(g).
   - It should waive any Event of Default arising from the Orrant Transaction.
   - Because §9.3 requires amendments and waivers to be signed by both Maker and Holder, the consent should be countersigned by both.
2. **Fallback: prepay the note.** §4.5 allows prepayment at any time without premium or penalty. The note could be paid off at or before the Orrant closing, funded at closing or through the MIPA purchase price mechanics.
   - Before paying in full, Baimix should consider withholding the disputed $1,150,000 (see Issue 2), but only under a negotiated arrangement.
3. **Coordinate with Orrant's counsel.** The consent (or payoff) should be a closing condition or a covenant under the MIPA, and the MIPA disclosure schedules should reflect this item.
4. **Use the consent negotiation as leverage.** Seller's consent is the main point of leverage available to Baimix. It is a natural vehicle for also resolving Issues 2, 3 and 4 in a single signed letter agreement. Under APA §11.11, a signed letter agreement referencing the APA ranks first in precedence.

---

### Issue 2: The July 20, 2026 claim notice missed the escrow Release Date and never reached the Escrow Agent

**Where it appears**
- Escrow Agreement §4.1, §4.2 and §9.1.
- Letter Agreement Recital B.
- Related provisions: APA §9.1, §9.6 and §11.11; Seller Note §5.

**What the documents say**
- **Release Date.** Under Escrow Agreement §4.2, the Release Date is "the date that is six (6) months following the Closing Date." Running from January 12, 2026, the Release Date was **July 12, 2026**.
- **Release mechanics.** On that date the Escrow Agent releases the entire Escrow Fund to Seller. The only amounts retained are the Claimed Amounts of Claim Notices "delivered to Escrow Agent prior to the Release Date."
- **Notice requirements.** Under §4.1, a Claim Notice must be delivered to the Escrow Agent, with a copy to Seller. Under §9.1, notices to the Escrow Agent are effective only on actual receipt.
- **What Baimix actually did.** Recital B of the Letter Agreement records that Baimix sent its claim notice:
  - dated **July 20, 2026**;
  - to **Seller only**, at Seller's APA §11.2 notice address;
  - asserting **$1,150,000** of Losses for breach of APA §4.11 (Sponsorship Contracts). The Losses relate to sponsor refund and make-good demands for activation deliverables that were allegedly not performed before Closing.
- **Seller's position.** Seller disputed the claim in full on August 14, 2026. Both parties reserved all rights.

**Why it matters for Baimix**
- **The notice did not preserve the claim against the escrow.** It was sent eight days after the Release Date, and it was never delivered to the Escrow Agent.
- **The escrow has most likely already been paid out.** The Escrow Agent's duties are purely ministerial (§5.1, §5.2), and it had no Claim Notice on file. It should therefore have released the full $3,000,000 to Seller on or about July 12, 2026.
- **The APA's longer survival period does not extend the escrow.** APA §11.11 makes each Ancillary Agreement control as to its own subject matter, so the Escrow Agreement's release mechanics govern escrow release. The 18-month survival period in APA §9.1 does not change that.
- **The claim itself is still alive.** It was asserted in writing well within the 18-month survival period (which runs to July 12, 2027). Under APA §9.1 it survives until finally resolved.
- **The result is that Baimix's $1,150,000 claim is unsecured.** Baimix must recover from Seller directly or by setoff against the note.
- **Interaction with Issue 4.** Seller may argue that the sponsor make-good demands are pre-closing Liabilities under Assigned Contracts. On that view they would be Assumed Liabilities under APA §2.3(a), which would weaken the claim further.

**Recommended fix**
1. **Confirm the escrow status.** Contact Calderline in writing to confirm whether, when and in what amount the Escrow Fund was released, and whether any balance remains.
2. **Seek a re-escrow.** Ask Seller to re-deposit $1,150,000 into escrow, or into a new escrow, pending resolution of the claim. This can be packaged with the Change of Control consent in Issue 1.
3. **Preserve setoff and withholding rights.**
   - APA §9.6 permits setoff against the Seller Note.
   - Seller Note §5.2 permits Baimix to withhold the amount claimed from any note payment that falls due while a claim asserted in good faith by written notice to Holder remains unresolved. The July 20 notice was given to Holder, so it satisfies §5.2.
   - The next principal installment is **$1,500,000 due January 12, 2027** (Seller Note §4.2(a)). Baimix may withhold $1,150,000 from that installment if the claim is unresolved by then.
   - Under §5.3, proper withholding is not an Event of Default.
   - This protection depends on the note not being accelerated first (see Issue 1). Any consent or payoff arrangement must preserve it.
4. **Continue the Letter Agreement process.** Pursue the Section 6 information exchange and the senior-level meeting with Seller.
5. **Fix the notice process going forward.** Adopt an internal notice protocol for future claims so that notices go to every required recipient, including the Escrow Agent where applicable.

**Do not** take the position that the July notice was timely or that it preserved the claim against the escrow funds. It did neither.

---

### Issue 3: The Letter Agreement removes Title (APA §4.7) from "Fundamental Representations"

**Where it appears**
- APA §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representations"), §9.1 and §9.5(a)–(b).
- Letter Agreement §3.

**What the documents say**
- **Original definition.** APA §1.1 defines Fundamental Representations as §4.1 (Organization), §4.2 (Authority), **§4.7 (Title to Purchased Assets)** and §4.19 (Brokers).
- **Why the definition matters.** Fundamental Representations receive three protections:
  - Under §9.5(a), they are excluded from the $3,600,000 Cap.
  - Under §9.5(b), they are excluded from the $300,000 Deductible.
  - Under §9.1, they survive for six years instead of 18 months.
- **The amendment.** Letter Agreement §3 "amend[s] and restate[s] in its entirety" the definition to read "Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.19." Section 4.7 has been dropped.
- **Precedence.** APA §11.11 ranks signed letter agreements referencing the APA first, and Letter Agreement §7.1–7.2 confirm that it amends the APA. The narrower definition therefore controls.

**Why it matters for Baimix**
- **What §4.7 covers.** Section 4.7 is Seller's representation of good title to the Purchased Assets, free and clear. It also covers sole ownership of the festival brands, trademarks, domain names and the ticketing and fan database.
- **Why that matters.** For an asset buyer, this is the core protection: it is what Baimix paid $30,000,000 to acquire.
- **Consequences of the amendment.** Title and IP ownership claims are now:
  - **capped at $3,600,000**, and that Cap is shared with all other general representation claims;
  - **subject to the $300,000 Deductible**; and
  - **barred after July 12, 2027**, which is 18 months after Closing, instead of January 12, 2032.
- **The timing makes this worse.** The same Letter Agreement records that domain names and social media accounts were not transferred at Closing. Title defects in the brand assets are therefore a real risk, not a theoretical one.
- **Orrant diligence.** Orrant will likely focus on the strength of the title protection it is inheriting.

**Recommended fix**
1. Negotiate a further signed letter agreement or amendment that restores the definition to "Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.7 and 4.19," with effect from the Closing Date. Under APA §11.6, the amendment must be signed by both parties.

### Issue 4: Uncapped Buyer exposure for Seller's pre-closing contract liabilities

**Where it appears**
- APA §2.3(a), §9.3(b) and §9.5(c).
- Compare Letter of Intent dated November 14, 2025, §3(a).

**What the documents say**
- **Assumed Liabilities.** APA §2.3(a) defines them to include "all Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts, *whether arising prior to, on or after the Closing Date*." The Assigned Contracts are the artist engagement, venue booking/license and sponsorship agreements.
- **Buyer indemnity.** Under §9.3(b), Baimix must indemnify Seller for all Losses arising from any Assumed Liability.
- **No limits.** Under §9.5(c), "Claims under Section 9.3(b) shall not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible."
- **The agreed deal.** LOI §3(a) contemplated that Baimix would assume "only liabilities under assigned contracts arising after Closing." It expressly excluded liability for any breach, default, act or omission of Seller at or before Closing.

**Why it matters for Baimix**
- Read together, these provisions make Baimix responsible, without limit, for Seller's own pre-closing breaches of the Assigned Contracts. Examples include unpaid artist guarantees, pre-closing venue damage claims and unperformed sponsor deliverables.
- Baimix must also indemnify Seller if a counterparty pursues Seller for those breaches.
- **Seller's indemnity does not offset this.** APA §2.4 and §9.2(c) cover only *Excluded* Liabilities, and these are Assumed Liabilities.
- **The July claim is exposed.** The sponsor make-good demands behind the July claim concern pre-closing activation failures, so Seller can argue they are Assumed Liabilities and that Baimix bears them.
- **The LOI does not cure the problem.** It is superseded and, apart from Sections 8–12, non-binding. It shows what was agreed but does not override the APA.
- **Orrant diligence.** Orrant will identify this as an open-ended liability of the target.

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend §2.3(a) by signed letter agreement so that it reads, in substance:
   > "all Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts to the extent arising after, and to be performed after, the Closing Date, excluding any Liability arising from any breach, default, act or omission of Seller at or before the Closing."
2. Make a conforming addition to §2.4. Pre-closing Liabilities under Assigned Contracts should be expressly listed as Excluded Liabilities, so that Seller's indemnity under §9.2(c) applies to them.
3. Use LOI §3(a) as evidence of the agreed deal in negotiations. Bundle this amendment with the Issue 1 consent.
4. If Seller refuses, at a minimum negotiate a cap on §9.3(b) exposure for pre-closing liabilities.
